newsitem.title: USA: Dlr's fall versus yen good news for U.S., Japan.
newsitem.headline: Dlr's fall versus yen good news for U.S., Japan.

text.p: The dollar's abrupt decline against the Japanese yen over the past week is welcome news for the United States and Japan, but it raises questions about how much further a fall they would be comfortable with.
Officials from both countries have called the dollar's drop -- it has fallen more than six percent from a peak of over 127 yen earlier this month -- desirable.
"It's good news," said one U.S. administration official, who declined to be identified.

Washington and Tokyo voiced concern last month that a continued rise of the dollar against the yen could end up pushing up Japan's trade surplus. Japanese officials even hinted that major nations might step in the currency markets to sell dollars to keep the greenback from appreciating.

In the event, they have not had to. Jawboning by Japanese officials, coupled with shifting expectations in financial markets about the outlook for U.S. and Japanese interest rates, have been enough to push the yen down.
The Japanese bond market has fallen sharply in recent days on fears that rock-bottom interest rates there may be heading higher.
U.S. bond prices, in contrast, have gained, as doubts have crept into the market about the likelihood of a rate increase by the Federal Reserve on May 20.
Japanese officials expressed some surprise at how abruptly the currency market has shifted gears and signalled their desire for the dollar to stabilize after its recent fall.
"The dollar is likely to settle down soon," Eisuke Sakakibara, Director General of the Japanese Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, said.
The U.S. Treasury Department, which overseas the administration's currency policy, had no comment on Monday on recent currency moves.

But one adminstration official said he believed that the Treasury would be comfortable with a dollar/yen rate roughly in the 110 to 115 yen. Other government departments, such as Commerce and the United States Trade Representative's Office, would probably prefer a weaker American currency, he added.
The U.S. Treasury first began showing signs that it felt that the dollar had risen enough back in September. At that time the U.S. currency was trading at about 110 yen.
That was the message that Japanese officials apparently delivered to the monthly meeting of central bankers from major industrial nations in Basle, Switzerland on Monday.

"We had a new assessment (of the Japanese economy)," Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer told reporters after the meeting. "Fears that fiscal drag could have a big negative impact seemed to be less now than before."

But U.S. officials said they were not so sure, noting that the weakened state of Japan's banking industry argues against much of a recovery there. "I don't see a strong recovery," one said, adding that what strength there is may stem from exports.
In late New York trading on Monday, the dollar was changing hands at about 119.50 yen.

Some Clinton administration officials remain sceptical about the soundness of Japan's economic recovery -- and that raises questions about how much further the yen can rise and how long-lasting its strength will prove.

The yen has risen in part because of a perception among investors that Japan's economy will not suffer as much as first feared from last month's increase in consumption taxes. That shift in investors' mood has helped spark a run-up in the Tokyo stock market.
